Surveillance · Brussels

Europe’s Chat-Scanning Law Reaches Its Last Room

Patrick Breyer counts down to a Tuesday-evening trilog on Chat Control, while the rest of the feed files its own evidence about who gets to read your messages.

By the Observer’s privacy desk

The EU regulation its opponents call Chat Control went into what Patrick Breyer describes as its final trilog on Tuesday evening, and the former MEP spent the window treating it as a deadline. On Monday he reported that people had marched in Warsaw on Saturday under the line Big Tech darf unsere Chats nicht überwachen! — Big Tech must not surveil our chats — and warned that Dienstag droht der finale Deal. By Tuesday morning it was a countdown: Bis 18 Uhr noch zum Telefon greifen! Phone your representative before six.

His ask is narrow and specific. Negotiators, he writes, must not accept “search plans” or mass scanning in the room tonight; he points readers at a list of delegates’ phone numbers and a press release arguing that EU governments want search plans to permanently legalise mass scanning. Breyer’s countdown · the Warsaw report

The outcome was not known when this edition closed. What the rest of the lens supplied, unprompted, was the case for caring. Eva Galperin, posting as evacide, linked a report that Meta Muse appears to read your Apple messages and upload them to the cloud even if you explicitly tell it not to. Source

The Electronic Frontier Foundation filed three times: a sticker campaign against licence-plate readers that opens Nobody wants to be on camera everywhere, all the time., an interview about the AI-integrated surveillance towers along the US–Mexico border, and a guide to shrinking your digital footprint. Signal, marking a year of Secure Backups, listed on-device backups, cross-platform support and attachment backfill for linked devices. EFF · the border towers · Signal

And the Cypherpunk Quotes account, which posts on a schedule and could not have known what day it was, reached back to John Gilmore in 1993: My response to the NSA is: Show us. Source

Dispatch · Kyiv

The Clinic Where They Took Their Son

Terry Yiu’s day in two posts: an attack on a hospital his family had used the week before, and a half-empty tank.

Terry Yiu reported on Monday that the Dobrobut medical center in Kyiv had been attacked. It was not an abstraction to him: We brought our son here one week ago for x-rays and were planning to schedule another appointment here. He added only: It's a very nice medical facility. So sad. Source

That evening the family went to fill up the car, which they keep topped up in case they have to leave at short notice. Two gas stations that we visited in Kyiv shut down in fear of being attacked. His sign-off is the most honest sentence in today’s paper: Tomorrow is another day, I guess. Source

Program, or Prompt?

The machines, and the children

A father’s question gets two answers from one household

hodlbod built his son a dungeon crawler and came away uneasy. Are you teaching your kids to program, or prompt? he asked, adding that I can't shake the feeling that I'm like a dad in the 90's teaching his kid to write assembly code. He is not handing the new tools over yet: I'm not about to unleash it on my kid. Source

Cyphernomad answered with a report from home, where the children write Minecraft mods, configure their systems with AI help, and edit config files in nvim. The two of them split exactly along the line hodlbod drew: My oldest prefers to prompt and take it from there, my youngest prefers to code and only let the AI do the tedious, boring stuff. Source

The grown-ups have already made their choice. ben, fifteen years a full-time developer: ive not written a line of code by hand this year. Source

Whose machine is doing the thinking?

Andrew M. Bailey set out a formal argument. Free expression is a condition of democracy; expression depends on deliberation; people now deliberate through machines they do not own, run by platforms whose values may not be theirs. His conclusion is open-weight models on your own hardware, and his slogan is the day’s best: Not your weights, not your mind. Source

WendyDing proposed a harder test for the science boosters: The real benchmark for AI for Science is not whether it can write a paper, but whether it can produce new, experimentally validated knowledge. Source

ngmi applied something like that test to a slime mould, feeding a Physarum network model to the decision model Jev across five experiments. In one of them, on 120 synthetic career personas, The adaptive result made decisions clearly worse. That is a negative result, reported plainly, which makes it rarer than a positive one. Source

The detectors, and the people they flag

Whitney Webb, who says she does not usually write opinion pieces, wrote one on AI “detectors” of AI-written text, arguing that they are not protecting human writing online. Source

Gigi went through it with a highlighter. Among the passages he marked in Webb’s essay was one about human writers now adjusting their style in order to please the Pangram gods, and one that ends: this is not a game that humans are meant to win. Source · Source

Flo Montoya’s answer came in marble, with four photographs of Albino Sirsi’s Oltre il velo (2022): In a world full of ai generated garbage, you can still choose the hand carved marble sculpture. Source

The European Commission, via a short video, would like it known that AI should help humanity, not harm it. Source

Custody

The day after

Everyone Is Talking About Coldcard, and Nobody Is Explaining It

Nothing in this window explained what happened to Coldcard. Everybody simply referred to it. Paula 33 promoted an interview with Tony Yazbeck by pointing to “the Coldcard hack” and a rise in wrench attacks. Source Watch out, Bitcoin! put a panel into Saturday morning’s programme in Madrid titled Cuando todo falla: el día después de Coldcard: when everything fails, the day after Coldcard. Source

Ungovernable’s hosts were asked which three signing devices they would pick for a two-of-three multisig. Max joked about three Coldcards on old firmware and then chose a SeedSigner and two Passports, with a caveat that is worth more than the list: I've not tested any other bits out, and I only wanna say what I'm comfortable with using myself. Q picked a Passport Prime, a Trezor Safe 7 and a Jade Plus. They agreed on the part that matters: Sparrow as the coordinator, and never all three from one manufacturer. Source

Cyphernomad, tired of custodial horror stories, drew a hard line: Want custodial, just buy the ETF and use a freaking bank account. And: It's self custody and banks. Everything else is just a mess. Source For anybody shopping, nostr.build released a hardware-wallet selector that filters by open source, secure element, multisig, air-gapped camera and known exploits, and Bitcoin Magazine reviewed the Trezor Safe 7. Selector · Review

The dollar comes to Lightning, and not everyone is pleased

Two headlines on the same Monday: Citi and Coinbase are building stablecoin infrastructure for businesses, and the Breez SDK has added a stablecoin feature. Citi · Breez

Kudzai Kutukwa’s long essay The Stablecoin Trojan Horse argues that the whole direction is backwards. Stablecoins, in his account, are fiat containers that inherit every failure Bitcoin was built to route around, freezes and blacklists included. He marked his own best line for emphasis: A dollar sent over Lightning is still a dollar. Essay · Highlight

TFTC picked up a question from Apollo’s chief economist, who asks whether AI agents might start a bank run by moving money out of low-yield checking accounts automatically. TFTC’s answer is that they will, and then keep going: Agents will help people get out of bad checking accounts. After that, it argues, they will help people out of the dollar itself. Source

From Quotable Satoshi, on a morning when heating season is starting across half the lens: The heat from your computer is not wasted if you need to heat your home. Source

The Workshop

What shipped

White Noise now has connectors that let AI agents, including Claude, Codex and OpenCode, message you in the same app you use for people. Max says the next release lifts group size from 50 to 200, And we still haven't worked on scale properly. The desktop client now runs on OpenBSD. Agents · Groups · OpenBSD

Max also posted a GrapheneOS tip: set third-party clipboard access to paste-only, so apps in the foreground cannot read your clipboard on their own. Source

LibreNostr 0.7.0 is a performance release: feeds render first and fill in names afterwards, and DM decryption has moved off the main thread. LWB shipped it from bed: Three days at home with a fever and we keep on building! Source

blossom-server 6.4, from hzrd149, with fixes contributed by others. Source

Sonar’s wallet is now Cashu. Vincenzo Palazzo’s release note is unusually careful about failure modes: a send the mint never answered stays pending rather than failing, and The fee on screen is the most that send will pay. A companion piece explains how reactions and local time now travel inside the encrypted chat instead of being published to relays. Cashu · Reactions

Blitz Wallet now runs in a browser, using the same keys. umbrelOS 2.0 is out, with a discount that ran until the 29th. Blitz · Umbrel

Pip called Sebastix’s nyves project one of the most ambitious and potentially impactful project on Nostr. Separately, Sebastix got a call from the Dutch parliament’s development department, which advised him to stay solo: keep it that way, it's the best way to do the work you love. Pip · Sebastix

The Reading Room

Long-form and technical

waxwing came across a Script trick he had not seen before. To commit to a small random number, you hash a random string whose length is that number, then reveal it: OP_SIZE on the preimage gives a 'little script' number directly. He traced it back to a 2013 paper on MPC on bitcoin. Source

tuco continues his OpenBSD series with an authoritative name server using NSD. Source
